newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ's Brash questions U.S. inflation target study.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ's Brash questions U.S. inflation target study.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash was quoted on Wednesday as challenging an argument by U.S. economists that zero inflation is an inappropriate target for monetary policy.
The Dominion newspaper interviewed Brash on the study by George Akerlof, William Dickens and George Perry of the Brookings Institution.
It summarised their argument as saying workers' resistance to cuts in nominal wages meant firms were pushed towards shedding jobs as inflation approached zero and their margins were squeezed.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand pursues a target of price stability, defined as zero to two percent inflation.
"My initial reaction (to the study) was, on the face of it, that the 0-2 is undesirably low if the Akerlof proposition is valid," Brash was quoted as saying.
However, he said there were three key arguments against the theory.
Continuing labour productivity growth meant that unchanged nominal wages rates would still produce a fall in unit labour costs over time.
Firms could also reduce wage bills over time as junior staff replaced senior, while wage rates remained unchanged.

Finally, overall remuneration was broader than wages. "There is much more scope for reducing an individual's total remuneration than there is in reducing the individual wage rate," Brash said, citing overtime rates and other perks such as health insurance.
Brash described Akerlof's conclusions as "suspect", the Dominion said. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
